top5.context:
Google's Gemini 4 Argon is now available in the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search
But only Google AI Ultra and Pro subscribers can access it for now.
By Mariella Moon
Oct. 13, 2026 12:00 pm EST
Google
Google's latest AI model, Gemini 4 Argon, is now available for more people. It first rolled out to members of Google's Fairwind Program, made up of governments and trusted partners that need access to the company's models with the most advanced cybersecurity capabilities, earlier this month. Now, developers can access it via the Gemini API and Google's agentic software developer platform Antigravity, while Google AI Ultra and Pro subscribers will be able to use it through the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search.
In the US, Google AI Pro costs $20 a month, while the Ultra tier costs at least $100. Access to Argon will set users back $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. But those are just introductory prices valid until November 30. After that, Argon will cost users double those amounts.
Google was supposed to launch a 3.5 Pro model, but it moved on and released Argon instead. The company said during its launch that the model can handle complex tasks involving finance, software engineering, coding, creative writing and cybersecurity defense. According to AI benchmarking company Artificial Analysis, Gemini 4 Argon matches OpenAI GPT-6 Astra's score for its Intelligence Index, which is its composite score for multiple AI benchmarks, at 60 percent of the cost per task at its introductory prices.
Josh Woodward, VP of Product for Gemini and Google Labs, said that in the Gemini app, Argon answers more quickly and with less hedging, repetitions and clichés. It can also return responses while it's still thinking when dealing with longer tasks that would usually mean waiting a bit — or a long while, depending on the AI being used — for results. Google is also making it easier to toggle between chat and tasks within the Gemini app. Plus, it's adding Antigravity's agentic coding interface inside Gemini's macOS app.

top5.title: Google Brings Gemini Personal Intelligence To Android Auto
top5.context:
Google brings Gemini Personal Intelligence to Android Auto
In the coming months, the feature will also roll out to cars with Google built-in.
By Igor Bonifacic
Oct. 20, 2026 4:00 pm EST
Igor Bonifacic for Engadget
At the start of the year, Google debuted Personal Intelligence, a Gemini feature that allows the chatbot to pull information from your other Google apps to generate more personalized responses. An expansion in March brought Personal Intelligence to free accounts after it was previously only available to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. And now Google has begun rolling out the feature to Android Auto users.
In practice, the company says today's update will improve Gemini's reasoning capabilities in cars. It will also make the assistant capable of delivering more specific details as they relate to your questions and prompts. For example, if you're driving to the airport, Google suggests Gemini with Personal Intelligence will be able to answer questions like "what's my flight gate?" and "is my flight on time?" Provided you've linked your Gmail account, it can do all this without you needing to pull over to find a confirmation email.
More broadly, Google says Personal Intelligence makes it easier to interact with Gemini more naturally. For instance, if you need directions to your doctor's office, you can just say "take me to my doctor's appointment," instead of speaking a specific address. Recommendations are also improved. If you're in a new city, Google suggests you can ask for dinner spots along your driving route and Gemini will generate suggestions while factoring in preferences and restrictions, like if you're a vegetarian.
As before, enabling Personal Intelligence is optional, and you can turn it off at any point if you don't want Gemini pulling your data. You can also control what apps Gemini can access. Google is starting to roll out Personal Intelligence to Android Auto users globally starting today (with the exception of those living in Switzerland, the European Economic Area, UK and Nigeria). In the coming months, the company plans to bring the feature to cars with Google built-in too.

top5.title: 5 Clever Ways Gemini Can Automate Everyday Tasks
top5.context:
5 clever ways Gemini can automate everyday tasks
Get the most out of Google's AI assistant.
By Filipe Espósito
Oct. 13, 2026 6:00 pm EST
Nwz/Shutterstock
AI chatbots like Gemini have become quite popular for their ability to answer questions, but they can do much more than that. When it comes to Google's Gemini, you can also use it to schedule and automate tasks without having to handle them manually every time. For example, you can ask Gemini to check your calendar every day to calculate how much time you'll have between appointments, or even to constantly check for updates on a specific website. And if you pay for Google AI Pro or Ultra, Gemini Spark can reach into your inbox and calendar too. Once you've set up Gemini, here are a few things you can try first to automate your daily tasks.
Check your day for travel trouble
Filipe Espósito for Engadget
As mentioned in the example above, Gemini is great for helping you manage your daily commitments. Ask it to check your calendars every morning and give you an estimate of how much time you'll spend moving between each event. Try a prompt like, "Check my events for the day and estimate total travel and driving time using Maps every morning at 7:30AM." Of course, this will only work if you have all the relevant apps — like your calendar and email — connected to Gemini. Just be aware that Google may not take real-time traffic data into account, since it will use the data it has at the time the answer is generated. It's always a good idea to check the route on Maps before you leave.
Get a daily briefing on the latest news
Filipe Espósito for Engadget
You can also ask Gemini to keep you up to date on a specific topic, like something you're personally interested in or monitoring for work. It can search the web at a set time and provide you with a summary of what it thinks is most important. A prompt like, "Every morning at 9AM, search for the latest news about Apple" is a good example. Google's own examples often feature daily and weekly summaries like this one. However, you can only run up to 10 scheduled actions at a time, so you might want to save them for important searches. You'll also receive a notification once your results are ready.
Plan the weekend before it starts
If you like getting suggestions for things to do on the weekends, Gemini can help you with that, too. Ask it to suggest an itinerary with different places to have dinner every Friday and Saturday. Give it access to your location so it knows where you are and can search for nearby places without you even having to tell it. It's a great way to discover new cafes and restaurants every week. Try a prompt like, "Every Friday morning, plan my weekend with different ideas for cafes and restaurants to visit." Scheduled actions will not use your current location if you're traveling — it will use the location it accessed when you first set up the action.
Turn repeat prompts into skills
With Gemini, you can also define a set of instructions using skills, which are replacing Gems, to remember preferences across different conversations. Let's say you're working on a weekly newsletter and you need to follow institutional brand guidelines to ensure that the content aligns with the brand's communications. Just create a skill with all the instructions, and use the command to trigger that skill. Every time you use it, Gemini will apply the brand guidelines you've defined without you having to list them every time you want to generate your newsletter. Using skills is as simple as entering a command like "/skillname" in your Gemini chat. Google says that soon you'll use the @ symbol to invoke a skill instead of /.
Let Spark handle your inbox
Koshiro K/Shutterstock
Gemini Spark is Google's always-on agent for AI Pro and Ultra subscribers, and it keeps working even when your phone and laptop are off. For example, you can have Spark scan your entire week's worth of emails and summarize the most important ones. Not only that, but it can also create a to-do list and automatically add any appointments to your calendar. No need to waste time doing all of this manually. Just make sure to connect it to Gmail, Calendar and Drive first — they're all off by default. It's as simple as going into the settings and flipping a switch on.
And don't worry, because Google says Spark is designed to check with you before taking any major actions, so it won't suddenly delete your important emails and files. One last thing: The availability of certain Gemini features may be limited to specific regions, so it's worth checking that as well.

top5.title: Singer or clanker? YouTube Music will tell you with new gen AI labeling. - Ars Technica
top5.context:
Genuine human creativity takes time, but you know what doesn’t? AI slop. There are countless AI models out there that can make something that passes for music, and you might come across those tracks on streaming services without realizing it. Google says it will begin labeling that content in YouTube Music, building on similar disclosures in the main YouTube app.
Google is not outright banning AI music or even speaking ill of it. “Generative AI is opening up new ways for artists to create, experiment, and share music,” the company says in a blog post.
However, the company also acknowledges that people want to know if a song was created with generative AI tools. A new label for AI content on YouTube Music is now rolling out in the app and on the website, which looks a lot like a label Google began adding to AI-generated videos on YouTube earlier this year.
The AI label will be visible on the player page, and a tap will open a menu with more information. The label will be applied to songs that were created entirely or altered significantly with AI. But how will Google know when to apply that label? That could be a little tricky.
The process of labeling AI music will be similar to Google’s detection setup with YouTube videos. Google says it is working with partners and using its own detection tools to identify AI music. When publishers upload content, they can specify how much (if any) gen AI was used. The tiers are fully gen AI, partially gen AI, and no gen AI. However, this is optional.
YouTube may also be able to detect AI usage without voluntary disclosure. In the case of tracks created using Google AI, there’s SynthID watermarking to indicate whether something was generated or edited with AI. It may also use C2PA metadata, which many other AI musicmakers use.
While Google is in a better position than most streaming services to spot AI content, the absence of a label should not be taken as proof that something is the product of human talent. This is true with AI labeling of all types of content. There are just too many ways to utilize AI tools, many of which leave no identifying mark in the resulting file.
Labeling AI tracks is a step in the right direction, but it may not be as useful as it is on YouTube videos. On YouTube, you’re probably looking at the screen and will see the AI label, but that is often not the case when listening to music. You’ll have to suspect something is amiss and check your phone or background tab to find out if what you’re hearing is AI-generated. There is no option to simply block labeled AI tracks from appearing in your playlists.
AI labeling for music is rolling out now in YouTube Music. Google notes that AI music uploaded as YouTube videos will get the same treatment soon.

top5.title: Singer or clanker? YouTube Music will tell you with new gen AI labeling. - Ars Technica
top5.context:
Genuine human creativity takes time, but you know what doesn’t? AI slop. There are countless AI models out there that can make something that passes for music, and you might come across those tracks on streaming services without realizing it. Google says it will begin labeling that content in YouTube Music, building on similar disclosures in the main YouTube app.
Google is not outright banning AI music or even speaking ill of it. “Generative AI is opening up new ways for artists to create, experiment, and share music,” the company says in a blog post.
However, the company also acknowledges that people want to know if a song was created with generative AI tools. A new label for AI content on YouTube Music is now rolling out in the app and on the website, which looks a lot like a label Google began adding to AI-generated videos on YouTube earlier this year.
The AI label will be visible on the player page, and a tap will open a menu with more information. The label will be applied to songs that were created entirely or altered significantly with AI. But how will Google know when to apply that label? That could be a little tricky.
The process of labeling AI music will be similar to Google’s detection setup with YouTube videos. Google says it is working with partners and using its own detection tools to identify AI music. When publishers upload content, they can specify how much (if any) gen AI was used. The tiers are fully gen AI, partially gen AI, and no gen AI. However, this is optional.
YouTube may also be able to detect AI usage without voluntary disclosure. In the case of tracks created using Google AI, there’s SynthID watermarking to indicate whether something was generated or edited with AI. It may also use C2PA metadata, which many other AI musicmakers use.
While Google is in a better position than most streaming services to spot AI content, the absence of a label should not be taken as proof that something is the product of human talent. This is true with AI labeling of all types of content. There are just too many ways to utilize AI tools, many of which leave no identifying mark in the resulting file.
Labeling AI tracks is a step in the right direction, but it may not be as useful as it is on YouTube videos. On YouTube, you’re probably looking at the screen and will see the AI label, but that is often not the case when listening to music. You’ll have to suspect something is amiss and check your phone or background tab to find out if what you’re hearing is AI-generated. There is no option to simply block labeled AI tracks from appearing in your playlists.
AI labeling for music is rolling out now in YouTube Music. Google notes that AI music uploaded as YouTube videos will get the same treatment soon.

top5.title: OpenAI Says It's Cutting Off Internet Access For Frontier Model Training
top5.context:
OpenAI says it's cutting off internet access for frontier model training
The company is trying to avoid another Hugging Face incident.
By Ian Carlos Campbell
Oct. 23, 2026 6:37 pm EST
Samuel Boivin/Shutterstock
OpenAI will train frontier AI models without internet access moving forward, the company announced in a blog post, in an attempt to protect internet infrastructure and limit other safety risks. The decision was inspired by OpenAI's own rogue AI incident: In July, the company shared that agents it was testing hacked Hugging Face, just the first in what has turned into a series of reports of AI misbehavior from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google.
"Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access," OpenAI says.
The company said that restrictions on what agents can access is "paramount" to its new approach. The company allows agents to access browsers, computer-use tools and code environments they need for training tasks, but in a secure environment that's not connected to the live internet. Communication is also limited to only agents with authorization.
OpenAI
Everything else remains out of reach, including the live internet, which the company says isn't necessary for training and "most evaluation." Because many of its recent models are meant to power agents like Dots, which browse and use apps for you, OpenAI built an "offline world" of indexed and cached web material for agents to use without touching live websites.
Even with those restrictions, OpenAI says the red-teaming agents it dispatched to test security safeguards found vulnerabilities that allowed them to escape the virtual machines (VMs) used to isolate agents from their host system. Agents also found a way to communicate with each other by manipulating data in a processor's cache and timing how long it took to load. To address both, OpenAI says it's disclosed and fixed vulnerabilities in several VMs and added checks to its monitoring systems to spot when models try to collaborate.
OpenAI paused frontier training in September. In announcing this new internet-free process, the company shared that it restarted training on October 1. OpenAI plans to continue frontier training without internet access until improvements in existing safeguards "justify broader internet access," but it didn't share what those improvements would look like.

ChatGPT now lets you lock sensitive chats behind a PIN
Locked chats aren't a form of end-to-end encryption, however.
By Igor Bonifacic
Oct. 20, 2026 5:05 pm EST
OpenAI
OpenAI is making it easier to protect your ChatGPT conversations from prying eyes with the introduction of a feature called locked chats. With it enabled, you can decide whether a past exchange appears in your regular chat history, pinned chats and conversation search. To access your locked chats, you'll need to input a 4-digit PIN. On an iPhone or Android phone, you can also use authentication systems like Face ID to access those conversations. Either way, you'll find your private conversations grouped under a new project titled "Locked chats."
OpenAI envisions locked chats mostly as a way to prevent people in public or someone you hand your phone to from seeing your conversations with ChatGPT. The company says so explicitly in a newly published support page, where it also notes locked chats won't automatically change your model training settings, or how long OpenAI retains your private conversations. That said, if you need to reset your account PIN for any reason, doing so will delete all of your locked chats, alongside any files you've uploaded to their project space. "This cannot be undone, and OpenAI Support cannot recover the deleted content," the company warns.
OpenAI says it's rolling out locked chats to users gradually. If you don't see the option right away, it may take a few days before it arrives in your account. top5.title: OpenAI answers TypeSafe's Jev with a Decision API built on Luna
top5.context:
OpenAI answers TypeSafe’s Jev with a Decision API built on Luna
With the sudden rise of TypeSafe’s Jev, decision models have become incredibly popular, so it’s not surprising that OpenAI is also announcing its take on this model type at its annual DevDay conference on Tuesday.
The company’s new Decisions API is based on the company’s Luna model — the smallest and most affordable model in its current lineup.
Limited preview
The Decisions API is likely a reaction to TypeSafe and Jev, and OpenAI probably rushed the announcement ahead of its DevDay, so for now, this is all OpenAI is sharing about the Decisions API.
An OpenAI spokesperson tells The New Stack that the company plans to share more “at broad rollout.”
For now, the new API is available in limited preview, and the broad release is planned for the coming days.
Predefined answers, real confidence scores
The core idea behind these decision models is that they are explicitly not chat models; instead, they return a set of predefined answers with confidence scores. Regular LLMs are not always very good at this. Their confidence scores, after all, are often a rough guess — and they burn quite a few tokens to get there.
This makes this kind of model ideal for classifying content, routing requests, or choosing an agent’s next action from a limited set of choices.
Decision models, however, can provide more realistic confidence scores, and they tend to return them extremely fast. OpenAI says its model returns results in 150 milliseconds, compared to GPT-6 Luna, which would take 1.6 seconds.
All the developer has to do is provide the questions, answers, and context.
OpenAI DevDay 2026 coverage:
Prompts vs. small classifiers
Today, most teams handle this today with a regular chat model and a carefully worded prompt, asking it to pick from a list and, if they’re lucky, reading the token probabilities to get something that resembles a confidence score.
The alternative is to train a small classifier. That is fast and cheap but needs labeled data and a retraining run every time the label set changes.
A decision model basically sits between those two options. It takes new labels in the prompt but returns a score a developer can work with.
This isn’t a completely new concept for OpenAI. Its Moderation API has long returned per-category scores instead of prose, too, though in this API, the categories are pre-set by OpenAI, not the developer.
What’s still unclear is what the Decision API costs per call, how many candidate answers a single request can handle, and whether developers can tune it on their own data. Those details will decide whether this becomes a standard building block in agent frameworks or stays a niche tool next to the chat models.

By Mariella Moon
Oct. 21, 2026 6:53 am EST

OpenAI's agents misbehaved by switching off the systems meant to monitor them for misbehavior, or in AI parlance, misalignment. In the latest post on the company's Alignment Research Blog, it reported two instances of agents weakening its misalignment monitoring systems while they were working on software changes.
In the first incident, a GPT-6.1 Sol agent disabled automatic alerts to OpenAI's security team. It happened on October 3, when a staff member asked the agent to create evaluation tasks using employee feedback collected via Slack. They told the agent, as part of the instruction, not to send any messages about the task. The agent used that instruction as the reason to stop sending the security team monitoring notifications. In another incident that took place on October 6, a GPT-6 Astra agent that was migrating a program removed OpenAI's monitoring system and then falsely told the user that it didn't disable it.
Last month, OpenAI canceled the launch of GPT-6.1 Astra, because it reportedly showed higher levels of deception than its predecessors during internal testing. The models involved in these cases are already available to the public, but they still displayed deceptive behaviors. Just imagine how much more deceitful GPT-6.1 Astra is for the company to pull its planned launch this month.
Both incidents happened during internal coding tasks and didn't result in a third-party website or service getting hacked. But OpenAI says it's making it harder for agents to disable monitoring, and it's also evaluating whether the cases mean its agents have the "propensity to evade misalignment monitoring." AI companies have promised to be better at preventing and reporting misalignment incidents involving their models and agents, after reports came out one after the other that they broke free from their isolated testing environments and infiltrated third-party services.
In OpenAI's case, it admitted back in July that the agents it was testing broke into AI repository Hugging Face. top5.title: OpenAI's ChatGPT/Codex desktop app is now on Linux
top5.context:
OpenAI’s ChatGPT/Codex desktop app is now on Linux
On Tuesday, OpenAI launched its ChatGPT desktop for Linux.
Now in preview, the app, which combines ChatGPT, ChatGPT Work, and Codex, will run on Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04 LTS, Debian 13, and Fedora 43 and 44, with native .deb and .rpm packages for both the x64 and ARM64 architectures.
The ChatGPT desktop for Mac and Windows launched in July when OpenAI introduced ChatGPT Work.
“Linux has been one of the most-requested platforms for the desktop app, and this launch extends ChatGPT and Codex across every major desktop operating system,” an OpenAI spokesperson tells The New Stack.
“Linux has been one of the most-requested platforms for the desktop app.” — OpenAI.
Like the ChatGPT desktop app on MacOS and Windows, the Linux version will feature OpenAI’s in-app browser and support for Chrome extensions.
One feature that won’t be available on Linux, though, is computer use outside of the in-app browser, as an OpenAI spokesperson confirmed to us.
“The Linux app supports the core ChatGPT and Codex experience, including Voice,” the spokesperson tells us. “The main difference is that native Computer Use — the ability for ChatGPT to interact with desktop applications like OpenOffice or GIMP — isn’t available at launch. This also affects related features, including Appshots, Record & Replay, and voice requests involving desktop apps and browser. Other browser-based workflows, including the Chrome extension, are supported.”
The app will be available globally at launch.
From Codex to ChatGPT app
Since the new ChatGPT app launched, the company refined the app a bit, given that the earliest version clearly felt like a rebranded Codex app with ChatGPT Work and the regular ChatGPT chat tagged on. In its current iteration, it’s easier to switch between ChatGPT and Codex, but for casual users, it’s likely still a bit of a confusing experience.
To be fair, Anthropic’s Claude app suffers from many of the same problems and finding the best user experience for working with agentic systems is clearly still a work in progress.
Chat interfaces have proven to work well when users want to ask a question and receive an answer. They become less natural when an agent is running for an hour, all while coordinating several subtasks, waiting for an approval, editing files, and/or producing multiple artifacts. At that point, the product needs to behave as much like a project dashboard as a messaging app.
More than a GUI for Codex
It’s worth noting that Linux users haven’t exactly lacked access to OpenAI’s coding agent.
The Codex CLI already runs on Linux, as does the company’s IDE extension, while Codex cloud offers another way to delegate coding work without installing a desktop client.
What the desktop app adds is a visual workspace for coordinating that work. Users can keep multiple projects and long-running tasks in view, inspect files and generated artifacts, review code changes, and move between local and cloud-based work. The app also brings OpenAI’s browser, plugins, and broader ChatGPT features into the same interface.
For developers who live in a terminal, the new app won’t necessarily replace the CLI. The CLI remains the more direct option for inspecting a repository, running commands, scripting repeatable tasks, and integrating Codex into CI.
The desktop app is aimed at the coordination layer around those tasks, particularly when several agents, repositories, or different kinds of work are involved.
The fact that it also includes support for ChatGPT Work for knowledge work and the ChatGPT chat is a nice bonus, though.

That earlier pilot was deployed to workers from across Uber’s various departments, including finance, operations, and product. Indeed, a majority of the early adopters — some 80% — were non-engineers, Sumanth Sukumar, Uber’s VP of engineering, told TechCrunch.
“They used it for a wide range of tasks: analyzing complex data from our operations to identify trends and develop recommendations; localizing training materials for different markets and languages; and building personalized interactive dashboards to manage their daily work,” he said.
Yet while the ride-share giant is now going all in on ChatGPT, it has not settled on exactly how employees will use it. “Our approach is to make powerful AI tools available across Uber while giving teams room to experiment,” Sukumar said. “For example, earlier this year we paired 30 AI engineers with teams across Uber and gave them two weeks to automate key parts of their job. Those ‘AI pods’ showed us how much opportunity there is when you combine technical expertise with a deep understanding of a particular job.”
Uber didn’t disclose how much it’s spending on the new rollout of the chatbot. Instead, Sukumar said the company will track how employees use the tool. “We’ll look at how employees are using the technology, the kinds of workflows they develop and how it helps them work more effectively. We’ll evaluate those outcomes and use what we learn to guide how we deploy AI across the business,” he said. Uber says OpenAI worked closely with the company on integrating the chatbot.
OpenAI has moved quickly to scale up its enterprise business as it competes with its chief competitor, Anthropic. Once known largely as a consumer brand, the ChatGPT creator has swiftly gained a loyal following with business customers, while other AI companies have struggled to keep up.

ChatGPT now lets you lock sensitive chats behind a PIN
Locked chats aren't a form of end-to-end encryption, however.
By Igor Bonifacic
Oct. 20, 2026 5:05 pm EST
OpenAI
OpenAI is making it easier to protect your ChatGPT conversations from prying eyes with the introduction of a feature called locked chats. With it enabled, you can decide whether a past exchange appears in your regular chat history, pinned chats and conversation search. To access your locked chats, you'll need to input a 4-digit PIN. On an iPhone or Android phone, you can also use authentication systems like Face ID to access those conversations. Either way, you'll find your private conversations grouped under a new project titled "Locked chats."
OpenAI envisions locked chats mostly as a way to prevent people in public or someone you hand your phone to from seeing your conversations with ChatGPT. What they aren't is a form of end-to-end encryption or a way to skirt OpenAI's legal obligations if you get in trouble with your workplace or the law. The company says so explicitly in a newly published support page, where it also notes locked chats won't automatically change your model training settings, or how long OpenAI retains your private conversations. That said, if you need to reset your account PIN for any reason, doing so will delete all of your locked chats, alongside any files you've uploaded to their project space. "This cannot be undone, and OpenAI Support cannot recover the deleted content," the company warns.
OpenAI says it's rolling out locked chats to users gradually. If you don't see the option right away, it may take a few days before it arrives in your account. Availability will extend to free accounts, as well as to those with Go, Plus and Pro subscriptions. On Android and iOS, you can use voice mode in combination with locked chats, though you can't lock your Codex conversations behind the feature.

top5.title: Google and AWS open new paths for PyTorch beyond Nvidia
top5.context:
Google and AWS open new paths for PyTorch beyond Nvidia
At PyTorch Conference North America 2026 this week, Google open-sourced TorchTPU, a native PyTorch stack for Google TPUs, now available on GitHub. AWS also launched TorchNeuron in public beta, its open-source native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium, also available on GitHub.
Both releases seem aimed at making it easier for developers to move beyond Nvidia GPUs, whose CUDA software ecosystem has long dominated AI development. But while Google and AWS’s new offerings do ease some of the challenges of switching hardware, getting top-tier performance still isn’t straightforward.
For developers eager for more computing options, it’s promising but somewhat disappointing.
Google wants to make TPUs more PyTorch-friendly
Google put TorchTPU in preview with select customers in April (PyTorch says Google’s been working on the project since mid-2025), teasing a simpler way to run PyTorch workloads on Google’s AI chips. PyTorch support has long been an awkward dance, so the new backend could make it easier to run existing models on TPUs.
Google says it wants to make its TPU software ecosystem more open and developer-friendly for the PyTorch community, as it works to make the chips a more practical option for developers already using PyTorch.
Developed in collaboration with the PyTorch team at Meta, TorchTPU allows developers to run existing PyTorch workloads without JAX dependencies in the runtime. This way, rather than requiring extensive code changes, developers can migrate existing workloads with only “trivial code changes,” according to PyTorch.
Specifically, developers can use eager execution to debug models and torch.compile to optimize TPU utilization and reduce memory overhead. 
The new PyTorch stack from Google and Meta comes alongside a slew of other products and integrations announced at the conference, which Google says are “designed to help you run PyTorch effectively on Google Cloud or in your own infrastructure.” Google also announced integrations involving Hugging Face, vLLM, SGLang, llm-d, TorchTitan, Ray and TorchRec, while contributing LiteRT to the PyTorch ecosystem.
AWS wants in, too
AWS’s release extends the same PyTorch-native approach to its own AI chips.
Like TorchTPU, TorchNeuron gives developers a way to natively experiment and build models with PyTorch — this time for Trainium, AWS’s portfolio of AI chips designed for deep learning training and inference workloads. The public beta supports Trainium2 and Trainium3 instances.
AWS says moving a model to Trainium can be as simple as switching to .to(‘neuron’) for eager execution. Compiled models also need the Neuron backend selected, either as the default or in a torch.compile call.
TorchNeuron also integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) — a bare-metal language and compiler for programming AWS Trainium and Inferentia NeuronDevices — so developers can create custom operators and optimize performance on Trainium. AWS and PyTorch have published more detailed guidance on the backend’s execution modes and performance tradeoffs.
Both are getting closer, but not there yet
While TorchTPU and TorchNeuron are notable steps forward in opening up more hardware choices for PyTorch developers, neither is a silver bullet.
PyTorch says a simple code change can get models running on TPUs, but peak performance can require TPU-specific optimization.
For distributed workloads, PyTorch says TorchTPU’s default Skinny Collectives approach can incur an end-to-end performance penalty of roughly 30–40% compared with an optimized approach because it prevents the XLA compiler from overlapping computation and communication.
For workloads seeking peak performance, PyTorch recommends additional tuning and production-grade stacks:
“Of course, for production workloads seeking peak performance we would absolutely recommend pursuing an optimal approach based on Pallas kernels and production-grade stacks such as vLLM-TorchTPU, SGLang-TorchTPU, or TorchTitan-TorchTPU, as examples.”
TorchNeuron is in public beta. In a separate blog post, AWS says teams can try Trainium with a configuration change instead of a code or model rewrite “in most cases,” leaving open which workloads need more changes.
In a case study, AWS describes how its Generative AI Innovation Center worked with AI research and technology company i14 to adapt its Laplace 3B model for Trainium2. The implementation required three changes: 1) using native PyTorch for the GLA attention kernel; 2) redesigning how Muon communicates; 3) compiling the sequential backward pass.
The releases give PyTorch developers more options beyond Nvidia GPUs. For now, moving existing code is easier than getting peak performance on unfamiliar chips.

top5.title: DeepSeek open-sources the inference engine behind its API. And Huawei gets equal billing with Nvidia.
top5.context:
DeepSeek open-sources the inference engine behind its API. And Huawei gets equal billing with Nvidia.
DeepSeek has open-sourced the inference engine it uses to serve its models in production, a step it said last year wasn’t yet practical.
Dubbed DeepInfer, the framework is designed to let developers run DeepSeek’s V4.1 Flash model on their own infrastructure, with many of the same optimizations the company uses behind its API. Support for future DeepSeek models is also planned.
“Running a model efficiently is a different matter altogether.”
DeepSeek has, of course, long made its model weights available for developers to download and run using third-party software such as vLLM. But running a model efficiently is a different matter altogether. The software that manages requests, distributes work across chips, and generates responses can have a significant impact on speed, throughput and computing costs. And so DeepInfer essentially gives developers access to DeepSeek’s own approach to those challenges.
“We’re sharing our production stack to help the community lower compute costs, reduce energy use, and make AI more affordable.”
‘Making AI more affordable’
Taking to X on Tuesday, DeepSeek said it was making its internal inference technology available to outside developers in an effort to bring down the expense of running large AI models.
“We’re sharing our production stack to help the community lower compute costs, reduce energy use, and make AI more affordable,” the company writes.
Released under the Apache 2.0 license, DeepInfer includes optimized computing kernels and communication libraries, including DeepSeek’s previously open-sourced FlashMLA, DeepGEMM, and DeepEP, alongside mechanisms for distributing inference across multiple chips. It also supports speculative decoding, a technique that speeds up response generation by predicting and verifying multiple tokens at once, and asynchronous scheduling to reduce the time processors spend waiting for new work. The framework also supports structured outputs, allowing developers to specify how model responses should be formatted.
Alongside DeepInfer, the company is also open-sourcing deepseek-recipe, a companion library that handles how API requests are converted into model inputs, and how the resulting output is processed into responses. Available for Rust and Python, it’s designed to help developers reproduce the behavior of DeepSeek’s official API when running their own deployments. The library was quietly released in September, with an updated version published on Tuesday.
The announcement comes just days after DeepSeek released an updated version of V4.1 Flash, called DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, touting improvements in coding performance and efficiency. That release coincided with the company making its in-house web search technology available to developers through new Search and Fetch APIs, as per The New Stack‘s report on Monday.
Why DeepSeek held back in 2025
DeepInfer goes further than DeepSeek’s previous plans to share its inference technology. Back in April 2025, the company published a document outlining its plans for its inference engine, explaining that it had considered releasing the entire system before deciding to contribute individual components and improvements to existing projects instead.
At the time, DeepSeek identified several obstacles. Its inference software had evolved from an early version of vLLM into a highly customized system, and the company questioned whether its relatively small research team could maintain another major open-source project. There were also practical difficulties in making the software usable outside DeepSeek’s own infrastructure.
“The engine is tightly coupled with our internal infrastructure, including cluster management tools, making it impractical for public deployment without significant modifications,” the company wrote at the time.
So what’s changed now, exactly? Well, DeepSeek hasn’t explained how it overcame those earlier difficulties, although the scope of the new release offers some clues. The DeepInfer documentation makes clear that the publicly available software currently supports offline inference, with “the core features needed for serving at scale,” as the company puts it. However, several components needed to operate a complete production service are still missing. These include a KV cache management system, infrastructure for separating different stages of inference across machines, and load balancing across replicas.
In other words, DeepSeek has opened up much of the engine responsible for running its models, while leaving developers to supply some of the surrounding infrastructure required to operate a full-fledged service. That narrower release may help explain how the company has made its technology available despite the challenges it identified last year.
Nvidia and Huawei, side by side
While the release of DeepSeek’s inference engine is significant enough in its own right, arguably the more interesting tidbit is the hardware supported from day one.
“Arguably the more interesting tidbit is the hardware supported from day one.”
Nvidia is included, as expected, though support is restricted to its SM100 architecture, used in Blackwell data center GPUs. Notably, the other supported platform is Huawei’s Ascend 950 NPU series, putting the Chinese chipmaker alongside Nvidia in DeepSeek’s list of compatible hardware. Older Nvidia architectures, including Hopper, are conspicuously absent.
This also ties back to DeepSeek’s published open-source plans from 2025. While the company was reluctant to release its entire inference engine at the time, it committed to working with hardware manufacturers ahead of future model launches, with the aim of making its models available across different chip architectures from day one.
US export restrictions have complicated Chinese companies’ access to Nvidia’s most advanced chips, adding another dimension to DeepSeek’s growing ties with Huawei. In September, Bloomberg reported that DeepSeek was planning to deploy at least 160,000 Huawei Ascend 950DT chips at a new data center in Inner Mongolia, specifically to run its models. The company has largely relied on Nvidia for training, although The Information reported in September that DeepSeek also plans to increase its use of Huawei chips for training, with deliveries expected as early as the fourth quarter.
Later that month, Reuters reported that DeepSeek and Huawei were collaborating on software tools intended to make Ascend processors easier to program, further underlining the company’s investment in Chinese AI hardware.
The Huawei inclusion has already attracted attention among the wider developer community. In a discussion on Reddit, one commenter singled out the two supported hardware platforms as a highlight of the news, while another pointed to DeepSeek’s origins in quantitative finance as a possible explanation for its technical expertise.
“Once again Deepseek shows how good high-frequency traders are at optimizing performance… On Ascend NPUs nonetheless!!,” the commenter wrote.
Another user seemingly poked fun at Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5, following reports that requests involving kernel programming for Huawei’s AI chips could trigger safeguards that redirect certain advanced AI development tasks to an older model.
“Don’t let Opus 5.5 see this! It will delete the Ascend support,” the user joked.
It is worth noting that feature support differs between the Nvidia and Huawei implementations. DeepInfer’s batch-invariant inference and deterministic sampling features, which help ensure reproducible outputs under specified conditions, are available only on Nvidia hardware. DeepSeek’s published performance measurements also use Nvidia GPUs, with four SM100 GPUs used for prefill and 64 for decoding, leaving open the question of how the framework performs on Huawei’s chips by comparison.
For developers without access to either chip family, the immediate value may lie in studying the newly available code and adapting its optimizations to other inference engines. For now, DeepSeek has given the wider open-source community considerably more of its inference technology to experiment with.

top5.title: Experts worry about Nvidia's AI chip sales in China and influence over Trump - Ars Technica
top5.context:
On its face, the recent summit between Donald Trump and China’s president, Xi Jinping, didn’t change much in the world of AI regulation. Export controls were not discussed, with neither country seemingly interested in making concessions. An already tenuous trade truce was temporarily extended for just two months, and looming US controls that could drop soon could easily end that and trigger China to retaliate by cutting off exports of rare earths, analysts expect.
However, in the background of these shaky talks, Nvidia appeared to notch a big win, as China is currently mulling relaxing controls and allowing some of its biggest AI firms to import perhaps millions more of Nvidia’s banned chips over the next year.
Sources familiar with China’s talks told The Information that China’s tech oversight arm, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, asked Alibaba and ByteDance to share plans to buy Nvidia’s RTX Pro 5500 chips. Although these are gaming chips, China asked firms to detail how they plan to use them, with expectations that chips could be put into servers to help power the country’s most in-demand AI models.
Increasingly, Trump looks to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang for advice on AI, but not everybody agrees that what’s good for Nvidia is good for the United States.
Already the world’s most valuable company, Nvidia would obviously profit enormously in a world where risks are downplayed, and both countries’ priorities remain powering rapid developments in frontier AI without pumping the brakes. Some critics worry that Nvidia’s profit motivations may be steering Trump’s thinking at a pivotal moment when it may matter how well a president actually understands the risks of a new technology.
Trump “completely aligned” with Nvidia
For Nvidia, a big goal since Trump took office was to open up more of China’s market so that Nvidia could start selling chips that were restricted during Joe Biden’s administration. Huang has blamed US export controls for cutting Nvidia’s share of China’s advanced AI chip market from about 95 percent to zero, The Information reported.
Trump was not an instant ally. Instead, he came into office asking “What the hell is Nvidia?” and rather than loosening Biden’s export controls, he initially tightened them further, most notably by banning exports of H200 chips to China. Trump was even thinking about breaking Nvidia up, expecting that stoking more competition among chipmakers domestically was crucial to America winning the so-called “AI race” with China.
But then he met Huang over dinner at Mar-a-Lago, where Trump said he “learned the facts of life” and understood that Nvidia as a firm is an “amazing” AI leader. Ignoring warnings from lawmakers and national security experts, Trump lifted the export controls on H200 chips, which China eventually allowed to be sold to some firms. Since then, Trump and Huang have appeared together in public repeatedly, and they regularly talk by phone, according to Stephen Witt, the author of The Thinking Machine: Jensen Huang, Nvidia, and the World’s Most Coveted Microchip.
In an interview discussing Huang’s influence over Trump, Witt told NPR that Trump’s recent claims—suggesting that it’s a “hoax” that AI might destroy humanity and that instead AI will be an economic boon—are “exactly Jensen’s talking points.”
“Jensen is now the president’s most influential adviser on technology issues,” Witt said. “The two have become quite close.”
Witt spent time with “tons” of people in the AI industry who share Huang’s views, he told NPR. And like Huang, they tended to downplay risks that software developers—including Nvidia’s biggest customers like Anthropic and OpenAI—are right now urging the White House to take seriously, he found.
“Most of the hardware people, most of the people who designed the networking equipment and the microchips, feel like Jensen does,” Witt said. “They tend to have a very low sense of risk regarding this technology. They just don’t see it.”
He said this debate has been going on between the two camps for the past 10 years, and “neither camp has moved at all.” With Huang growing closer to Trump, it seems likely the president will continue downplaying leading AI firms’ warnings and avoiding serious talks with China about their models’ risks. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed ahead of Trump’s talks with Xi that “the president is completely aligned with Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia.”
Nvidia downplays risks
According to The Information, if China lifts export curbs on Nvidia’s gaming chips, it “would give Nvidia perhaps its best chance in more than a year to regain some momentum in China’s AI market.” If China gives the nod, ByteDance plans to order 1 million chips, which would automatically secure for Nvidia two quarters of projected sales.
That would certainly help improve Nvidia’s financial outlook in China, as China’s delayed approval of H200 sales meant sales were dismal, comprising less than 1 percent of Nvidia’s data center revenue in the most recent quarter.
Andrew Yoon, a researcher at an AI safety nonprofit called CivAI, told CNBC that in the AI industry, “Nvidia is the most aggressive in terms of, let’s just make money.”
“At every turn, they are really trying to just make sure whatever happens is good for Nvidia’s bottom line,” Yoon said.
If the US and China continue to loosen controls, some experts fear that too many chips may end up being diverted to China. Eventually, that could cause US data centers to lose a precious domestic chip supply that’s currently making it possible to stay ahead on frontier AI, the thinking goes.
Nvidia’s reporting suggests that as of now, the countries don’t compete for resources, though. In the first half of 2026, Nvidia reportedly took a $400 million hit due to vast quantities of unsold H200 chips. No American firms want those chips, since they can access Nvidia’s more advanced chips.
However, demand for chips made for China’s market could perhaps change, as more US data centers come online, policy experts believe.
Nvidia’s spokesperson told Ars that it China lifts curbs on “outdated” gaming chips “released nearly a half a decade ago,” it will only benefit US firms unfairly burdened by restrictions on chips that cannot be used to train AI. The statement recalls Huang’s remarks at a recent “All-In” summit hosted by Trump’s former AI czar, David Sacks. Huang publicly promised Trump: “We’re going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race of America. Every industry, every company, every state, every people.”
Yet, Witt joked that “Jensen is really the only one who wants to sell his equipment to China.”
Witt thinks that a responsible US president would set up a group like the National Transportation Safety Board to review mandatory reports of AI safety incidents. That could support the US-China safety alert system announced last week, which right now troublingly includes no tech experts. But that likely won’t happen, since “Jensen has convinced Trump that what’s good for Nvidia is good for America,” Witt said.
It remains unclear if China will approve the gaming chip sales, but sources told The Information that the government intends to allow at least some into the country. The pressure may be on to approve them, since “Chinese companies are rolling out AI products and services faster than they can find the chips to run them,” The Information noted. At least one buyer “plans to put eight RTX Pro 5500s in each server, a standard setup that lets the chips work together on larger AI models,” sources said. Supposedly, Nvidia is preparing to ship the first orders this December.
If Huang gets his way, Chinese firms will buy millions more of Nvidia’s chips in the coming years, helping the firm maintain global dominance over companies that are locked in on advancing AI.
Huang’s influence over Trump may be tested
During the most recent summit between Trump and Xi, Huang joined many US tech leaders at a state dinner, including Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Sam Altman, Mark Zuckerberg, and Satya Nadella. Noticeably, China invited none of its tech leaders.
Ro Khanna, the top Democrat on the House of Representatives’ select committee on China, told The Guardian that Trump could have used the tech leaders’ help to press Xi in their talks to set up technical working groups to monitor AI threats. But Trump seems to have “no interest in doing that,” Khanna said.
At the summit, Xi acknowledged that the US and China have the “responsibility to develop and manage AI for good” and “ensure that the development of AI is always under human control,” The Guardian reported. But neither country was willing to make “even a symbolic gesture” that an AI slowdown may be necessary if risks cannot be contained.
Jonathan Czin, a fellow in the China Center at the Brookings Institution, told The Guardian that he had “very low expectations going into this meeting for anything of substance, and the meeting managed to underwhelm even those low expectations.”
“Even going into this meeting, you’re dealing with a septuagenarian and octogenarian who may or may not have ever had first-hand contact with actually using AI, and what happens with this technology rests on their two shoulders,” Czin said. “The only thing they seemed to agree about is that neither of them wants to slow down with this technology, regardless of their actual understanding of it.”
Trump may soon have to reconcile the differences between some of Huang’s views on AI safety and his own law enforcement, however. While the FBI has accused six Chinese firms of aggressively copying US frontier models, Huang has sided with China, arguing that distillation of frontier AI models is “not robbery” but rather “competition,” CNBC reported.
“You’re allowed to test somebody else’s products all you want,” Huang said, suggesting that AI firms could disable services to block distillation if they wanted. He further noted that “Nvidia’s products are sometimes stripped ‘down to bones’ as companies tried to learn how they worked.”
“I’d really prefer they didn’t,” Huang said. “I’d really prefer that nobody learns from our products, and we have the benefit of just cruising along. But, you know, frankly, competition makes everything better.”
To Huang, getting Trump to agree with him might be easy, Witt suggested. As he explained:
When I interviewed Jensen years ago, he told me that every problem in the world is actually an engineering problem. Now, that’s true if it’s a personal problem or a business problem or a political problem. You study the inputs and then you modify the inputs to get the outputs that you want. In this case, I think Jensen has realized that the inputs for Trump are, like, flattery—like, public flattery, nonstop public flattery. And the outputs are, you know, lifting restrictions on sales of Nvidia equipment to China and zero regulation on AI.
Despite Bessent’s suggestion that Huang is pulling the strings, Trump took to Truth Social ahead of the “All-In” summit to make it clear that he expects to be trusted as the sole authority when it comes to AI safety.
“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Trump wrote.

top5.title: US arrests tech CEO accused of smuggling $300M in Nvidia chips into China - Ars Technica
top5.context:
The US has arrested another suspect accused of smuggling high-end computer servers containing export-controlled Nvidia chips into China.
In a press release on Thursday, the Department of Justice accused 38-year-old Greg Lui of using false paperwork to mask shipments of servers worth more than $300 million that he allegedly knew were ultimately destined for China.
As the CEO of Earthmade Computer, Lui allegedly conspired with freight-forwarding firms in South Asian countries like Malaysia and Singapore to illegally divert chip shipments into China, including Nvidia’s A100 GPUs and H100 GPUs, the FBI’s indictment alleged. These are not Nvidia’s most advanced chips. However, the chips can process large amounts of data and train large language models, which the US fears could pose national security risks if China suddenly gets access to enough chips to drastically advance its AI or strengthen its military.
Emails and bank records exposed the smuggling scheme, the DOJ alleged, which started in October 2023 and continued until August 2026.
One key piece of evidence is a 2024 email discussing an order for 70 servers with export-restricted GPUs that were fraudulently claimed as destined for Malaysia. After “Lui submitted a purchase order to a US manufacturer for 27 of these servers for approximately $7,614,000,” the DOJ alleged that a co-conspirator told a Malaysian government official that all 27 were shipped to China.
A similar shipment of 92 export-controlled servers was allegedly routed through Singapore to Malaysia, then Hong Kong. Finally, the chips went to a Chinese firm based in Hangzhou, the FBI alleged, which The Wall Street Journal last year described as China’s AI hub.
Yet another flagged 2024 shipment shows how far Lui allegedly went to fool US officials.
When shipping 100 Malaysian-bound servers—each containing Nvidia H100 GPUs worth over $22 million—Lui allegedly submitted fraudulent documentation from a fake buyer identifying its CEO as “Jackie Lui.” Three years prior, Lui “purchased the identifying documents of an individual whose identity is known to the grand jury and used this identity to conduct business transactions in furtherance of the export evasion scheme,” the FBI alleged.
In 2024, Lui’s firm allegedly received more than $176 million from the scheme. Payment records from Lui’s accounts with Bank of America and JP Morgan provided further evidence of how he allegedly operated the smuggling business.
Arguing the evidence backs the charges, the DOJ wants to seize all funds gained through the scheme. Arrested on three counts, Lui is accused of conspiring to violate the Export Control Reform Act and the Export Administration Regulations, as well as federal smuggling and money laundering laws. He faces up to 20 years in prison if found guilty of either the conspiracy or money laundering counts, and the smuggling charge carries a maximum penalty of up to 10 years.
Nvidia denied seeing red flags
Lui’s arrest comes after an Nvidia senior manager based in Taiwan was linked to a similar smuggling scheme allegedly run by ex-Supermicro staff in that country.
At that time, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang urged Supermicro to fix its compliance problem while claiming there was no evidence of smuggling. Since then, as more arrests have followed, Nvidia has pivoted from denying smuggling to downplaying the role smuggled chips and servers play in China’s AI industry, which is now largely powered by Huawei chips. On Thursday, a spokesperson told Bloomberg that “less than one half of one percent to Nvidia products” have allegedly been diverted to China.
“Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has,” Nvidia’s spokesperson said.
Experts suggest that the black market is “hard to measure,” though, and likely much bigger than has been reported.
Increasingly, Nvidia faces questions about its own “blind spots” when it comes to compliance with export controls, according to a lengthy Bloomberg investigation “based on conversations with dozens of people across five countries.”
Officials around the world suspect that hundreds of thousands of AI chips are being exchanged in a sprawling shadow trade likely powering small data centers and potentially even “a handful of hyperscalers” in China. These chips could fill a hardware gap that China doesn’t expect to address on its own until 2030, one “top executive” told Bloomberg.
Rushing to cut off the supply, US officials want Nvidia to voluntarily tighten its protocols and flag more suspicious shipments. That way, the chips don’t end up going to leading Chinese firms that Donald Trump has accused of stealing US technology to quickly expand Chinese AI capabilities, like DeepSeek.
“Government officials and industry experts are increasingly pointing to gaps in Nvidia’s due diligence, questioning how the company failed to catch red flags,” Bloomberg reported. Officials suggested the most scrutinized shipments ought to be facilities in Thailand, Malaysia, and Singapore.
Nvidia screens buyers and has blocked shipments when end buyers are unknown, but it’s not detecting seemingly obvious fraudulent shipments that some US officials think could easily be flagged.
For example, Nvidia and Supermicro visited a Taiwanese facility that bought high-end chips that were quickly passed on to a Chinese firm. Eventually, Taiwan’s Coast Guard “noticed discrepancies in shipping manifests,” Bloomberg reported, and seized the bulk of export-controlled servers. However, the FBI alleged that Nvidia could’ve stopped the shipments before they started since the facility “was clearly insufficient to house all the ordered servers.” Instead of exercising “basic scrutiny,” both chipmakers authorized the deal anyway, Bloomberg reported. Even more alarming, in another case, Nvidia didn’t notice that a small data center in Thailand diverting chips was relying on fake leases to purchase bulk orders. Nvidia won’t comment on whether that site was ever visited, Bloomberg noted.
Nvidia disagrees that it could’ve thwarted shipments officials have flagged. A spokesperson told Bloomberg that “a startup’s growth plan in a friendly nation is an opportunity for America, not a ‘red flag’ to be feared.” Most likely, Nvidia won’t turn down orders that don’t seem to fit existing facilities, since “Nvidia-powered servers are financeable asset that help startups secure capital and infrastructure, including data center space,” the spokesperson said.
Most glaringly, Nvidia continues to work with at least one entity that the US has recently flagged as potentially evading export curbs. Nvidia told Bloomberg it wouldn’t comment on whether it has conducted the urgent checks the US government requested to ensure Megaspeed wasn’t diverting tens of thousands of excess AI chips into China. The company will keep working with Megaspeed until it’s ordered to stop, the spokesperson said.
“When the law is clear, American companies honor US laws as they are, not as America’s critics wish they were,” Nvidia’s spokesperson said.
Rather than scrutinize its customers’ orders in countries neighboring China, Nvidia chose instead to make “an internal whitelist of Asian firms pre-approved for AI chip purchases,” sources told Bloomberg.
Nvidia wants more chips in China
Overall, Bloomberg’s report suggested that unless the US specifically bans sales or requires actions, Nvidia will continue doing business that ensures its AI chips dominate the market and power the world’s leading AI models.
Stricter rules are unlikely to follow, despite some calls in Congress to pass laws cutting off China from more chips. Industry opposition already watered down one anti-smuggling bill, Bloomberg noted, and Huang recently snubbed a congressional invitation to testify on the problem.
Additionally, Huang’s growing influence over Trump has spurred the president to similarly relax more export controls. So far, the Trump administration has been happy to let Nvidia police itself while moving slowly to block suspicious shipments, sources told Bloomberg.
That hands-off approach aligns with Trump’s general strategy for combating AI risks. The president is so determined to win the so-called AI race that he won’t put any meaningful guardrails on the industry. Meanwhile, polls show most voters want stricter AI regulations ahead of the mid-term elections.
Critics worry that Trump’s most recent attempt to rebrand “artificial intelligence” (AI) to “super intelligence” (SI) will only confuse the public even more about AI risks, while serving primarily to make Trump feel like the US has already achieved a milestone in AI that is, in reality, quite far off.
With US firms like OpenAI seemingly losing control of their frontier models, Trump’s understanding of AI risks also continues to draw scrutiny.
But Trump wants to be trusted as the sole authority on AI, no questions asked. At a recent United Nations assembly, Trump claimed his rebrand is simply because the president thinks the word “artiﬁcial” makes the technology sound “fake,” the South China Morning Post reported. He’s used security scandals to argue that frontier AI now goes beyond “merely imitating or automating aspects of human intelligence” and that supposedly makes “super intelligence” a “better reﬂection” of American AI firms; “growing capabilities and potential,” SCMP reported.
Trump officials have already adopted SI as a preferred term. In the DOJ’s press release, Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg declared that “SI is the defining technology of the era.” Even though AI leaders know the term is technically inaccurate, CEOs like Huang and Elon Musk have also committed to using SI.
Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, told SCMP that Trump’s just trying to project American dominance while ignoring risks. By overhyping today’s AI, the president hopes his rebrand will tie his legacy to the moment AI exceeded human capabilities.
Chan joined California governor Gavin Newsom in warning that the rebrand risks heightening “some people’s perception of risk and fear” amid frontier AI firms claiming that the technology could soon pose existential risks.
Newsom outright rejected Trump’s rebrand—describing it as an “impotent and craven failure to address well-documented emerging security and safety risks.”
And “respectfully,” so does China’s foreign ministry, SCMP reported. Both governments have immense influence over AI regulations and will continue using AI, not SI.

Machine learning is an application of artificial intelligence (AI) that assists in predicting future outcomes. Machine learning is being used across many industries, from fraud detection to business process automation. Machine learning gives companies a different view of their operational patterns and trends in customer behavior.
The machine learning framework moves beyond the traditional model of computation. Instead of arriving at a definite reproducible answer through a series of calculations, machine learning — a branch of artificial intelligence — works on a series of statistical probabilities to suggest new solutions to a problem. This work is useful for such jobs as designing new materials, medical diagnosis, advanced game graphics and so many other tasks.
What Is Machine Learning?
Machine learning (ML) is part of artificial intelligence (AI) which assists various applications in predicting futuristic outcomes more accurately. Machine learning is being used in many industries and for a variety of purposes from fraud detection to business process automation. Enterprises gain a different view of operational patterns within the organization and trends in customer behavior through machine learning implementation.
Machine Learning Techniques Are Used to Train Algorithms
There are four types of algorithms and several techniques used in machine learning. These types — supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised, and reinforcement learning — and their respective techniques are examined below:
Supervised Machine Learning
Much of the early success in machine learning has come from supervised learning, where a clearly defined data set is already available for analysis. The algorithm then determines how to arrive at given outputs and inputs. The machine learning algorithm makes predictions by analyzing the data and is corrected by the operator until its predictions are highly accurate.
In supervised machine learning, the algorithm learns through these three techniques:
Classification. The machine learning program determines what categories new observations belong to based on the analysis and observation of the available data sets.
Regression. The machine learning program estimates the relationship between variables where there is one dependent variable and a number of changing variables.
Forecasting. This involves making predictions about the future from new and existing data. It is also used to analyze trends.
Gathering recent momentum has been the Deep Learning technique, which doesn’t require all the intermediate steps that supervised learning does. Instead, the idea is to let the Deep Learning neural nets find the answers on their own.
Machine learning can be used for many different applications and industries, including operations. Find out more about Machine Learning for Operations.
Semi-Supervised Learning
Machine learning algorithms are provided with labeled and unlabeled data. Labeled data provides information about a given data set that helps the algorithm understand what the data is about. Unlabeled data has no descriptions. Through semi-supervised learning, machine learning algorithms learn to label unlabeled data.
Unsupervised Machine Learning
In an unsupervised learning process, the machine learning program is left to observe and analyze large data sets by determining the relationship between variables. There is no operator to make corrections and the algorithm solely addresses data accordingly. As it assesses more data sets, its deductions improve and become refined.
In unsupervised machine learning, the algorithm learns through these techniques:
Clustering. Based on defined criteria, the machine learning program groups similar data from a set by finding a pattern. Clustering is done when each data group needs to be segmented and analyzed.
Dimension reduction. Through predetermined criteria, this process reduces the number of available variables to find the required information.
Reinforcement Machine Learning
In reinforcement machine learning, algorithms are given specific actions, parameters, and results. The algorithm determines the rules and develops different processes for arriving at the given conclusion. The machine learning algorithm arrives at the result through trial and error. Through reinforcement, algorithms learn based on past experiences and adopt the optimal approach determined in new situations.
Top Machine Learning Technologies Are Transforming Ideas
Artificial intelligence technologies are improving outputs in machine learning. Through technology, operators can develop automated machine learning algorithms and achieve more in less time. Some new technologies train machine learning models and others such as Google’s Auto ML Zero — a new kind of automated machine learning — use simple methods to create algorithms that can be adapted to a task at hand.
RapidMiner: an automated ML tool that can significantly reduce the time needed to create predictive models for businesses across many industries with various resources and sizes.
Big ML: technology that automates the machine learning pipeline.
DataRobot: an automated ML tool leveraging regression techniques, neural networks, and gradient boosting to solve multi-class classification problems.
Auto Keras: an open-source software library designed to improve the creation of deep learning techniques
H20: technology that uses its own algorithms to create and optimize pipelines. This is achieved through exhaustive search.
TPOT: AI technology that uses genetic algorithms to optimize machine learning pipelines.
TensorFlow: an open source machine learning framework created by Google that is easy to deploy across various platforms.
Scikit-learn: an open source library developed for machine learning featuring several ML techniques.
Machine Learning Use Cases Are Expanding
Machine learning has many potential applications and is growing rapidly. The exponential growth of data contributes to the expansion and use of machine learning. Not only can machine learning be applied to client-facing applications like product recommendation, customer service, and forecasts, but it can also be used by internal teams to speed up processes and time-consuming tasks.
Here are some machine learning use cases today:
- Fraud detection
- Dynamic pricing
- Product recommendation
- Email filtering
- Personalized marketing
- Process automation
- Improving sustainability and the environment
- Proactive help desk operations
At The New Stack, we have focused our coverage of this emerging field mostly around two areas of scalable architecture. We are keeping a close eye on the emerging field of AIOps, where machine learning can influence and drive IT operations. AIOps help to automate the path from development to production, predicting the effect of deployment on production and automatically responding to changes in how the production environment is performing. Companies such as New Relic, OpsRamp, and Moogsoft have all invested heavily in this area.
Another area of machine learning we are covering closely is how Kubernetes and related cloud native technologies can expedite the machine learning lifecycle. Machine learning involves an entire IT cycle of technologies that are very early on in terms of commercialization. Data must be harvested and cleansed, models must be tested, and the most useful approaches must be pressed into production, with a feedback loop of some sort to ensure the models can be updated. Emerging workflows such as Kubeflow and Anaconda can help streamline these processes.

top5.title: Uber rival inDrive eyes 2027 robotaxi tests in Central Asia with Pony AI and Nvidia | TechCrunch
top5.context:
Ride-hailing company inDrive, known for letting passengers and drivers negotiate fares, is working with Chinese autonomous driving firm Pony.ai and Nvidia to begin testing robotaxis in Kazakhstan in 2027.
The companies said Friday that they had signed a memorandum of understanding to explore bringing Pony.ai’s robotaxis to inDrive’s platform — a reflection of the growing interest in self-driving technology beyond the U.S. and China.
Testing will begin in Kazakhstan’s capital, Astana, in the first half of 2027, inDrive CTO Yuri Misnik told TechCrunch. The tests will initially involve a safety operator, with fully driverless rides as the eventual goal.
Under the proposed plan, Pony.ai would provide its Gen-7 robotaxis, which inDrive would offer through its ride-hailing app and operate in Kazakhstan. Nvidia, on the other hand, would supply the AI technology, including its Hyperion platform and Halos safety system.
The move comes as ride-hailing companies expand their push into robotaxis. Earlier this month, Uber announced plans to test Pony.ai’s robotaxis in London, where it has also started offering supervised autonomous rides with British startup Wayve, an investor-backed partner. Uber is also working with multiple robotaxi companies in other markets, including the Middle East.
Having built its business around affordable rides, inDrive is now looking to bring a similar focus to autonomous ride-hailing as it explores a market where Uber and other rivals are already making moves.
“Our approach is capital-light by design,” said Misnik. “We work with a range of partners in different markets, combining their expertise with ours to deliver a better customer experience.”
Nvidia says its Hyperion platform could lower the cost of developing robotaxis by giving companies a ready-made foundation of sensors and computing technology, rather than requiring them to build and integrate everything themselves. The company also offers its Alpamayo model and tools to generate synthetic data and test autonomous driving systems across different driving scenarios.
“Those savings are particularly relevant in emerging markets, where ride-hailing is already relatively affordable and autonomous services need to compete on cost,” Ali Kani, Nvidia’s vice president of automotive, told TechCrunch.
The announcement coincides with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s first visit to Kazakhstan on Friday.
The Kazakhstan proposal would also add to Pony.ai’s ongoing push beyond China. The company aims to have more than 3,500 robotaxis operating in over 20 cities worldwide by the end of 2026, up from a fleet of 1,975 vehicles at the end of June.
Last month, Kazakhstan announced plans to launch autonomous taxi services in 2027, with initial trials planned in Astana and two other cities. It has also introduced rules for autonomous vehicles to be tested on certain public roads.
Astana’s harsh winters could make it a useful testing ground for robotaxis. The city, with a population of around 1.7 million, faces months of snow and ice, posing challenges for autonomous driving systems.
“Launching here will provide an important opportunity to evaluate autonomous driving technology in challenging winter conditions,” inDrive founder and CEO Arsen Tomsky said. “Success in Astana could offer valuable insights for expanding autonomous mobility to other locations facing similar challenges.”
Kazakhstan is not the only market where inDrive is exploring robotaxis. In December, the company signed a separate agreement with Saudi Arabia’s AI Driver to explore deploying autonomous vehicles powered by Chinese self-driving firm WeRide, starting with Riyadh. The companies had targeted a pilot in the first half of 2026, though it remains unclear whether testing has begun.
“We are also looking at a number of other markets for future deployments,” said Misnik. “One of the main requisites for successful launch in our view is a favorable and collaborative regulatory environment to facilitate safe and sustainable testing on the roads.”
The company operates in more than 1,200 cities across 47 countries and has expanded beyond ride-hailing into delivery, intercity transportation, and financial services.
