top5.title: Tesla starts Optimus robot production in California as profit falls 43% | TechCrunch
top5.context:
Tesla has started production of its Optimus humanoid robot at its factory in Fremont, California, in a manufacturing space once dedicated to making electric vehicles, the company announced Wednesday.
“The bots coming off this line are the first production-quality bots that we have manufactured,” Tesla wrote in its third-quarter letter to shareholders. “While we will continue to iterate on the hardware and manufacturing process, we have proven that the current manufacturing process for Optimus is suitable for a commercial product.”
Tesla CEO Elon Musk said on a conference call that he considers this “early production” and that the ramp will be slow and “somewhat bumpy because it is such a radically new product.” He nonetheless claimed Tesla will be able to make 20,000 of them per week by the end of 2027.
“There’s still some things we need to tweak about the design, because you need to deliver a robot that is safe and reliable and has long duration, so it can’t, like, wear out after a month,” he said. “And there’s still quite a lot of work to do with regard to the AI and the robot for it to be truly useful for open-ended tasks.”
That forward-looking development wasn’t enough to lift the company’s otherwise middling third-quarter earnings, results that typify a company in the midst of a major bet. Tesla’s revenue was flat and its expenses skyrocketed as it pressed the accelerator on its Optimus robots, AI, and autonomous driving. The end result was a 43% drop in profits.
The company’s revenue was largely driven by EV sales, which were flat year-over-year at $20 billion. Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in the third quarter, about 6,000 more than the previous quarter, but fewer than in the same period last year.
Tesla’s total third-quarter revenue was $28.04 billion, a skosh below the $28.09 billion it generated in the third quarter of 2025. Tesla’s third-quarter revenue was also about $200 million lower than the previous quarter’s haul of $28.23 billion.
Tesla saw a 16% year-over-year decline in revenue from its solar and energy storage business to $2.8 billion, which it blamed on tariff-related customer refunds. There was some positive revenue growth in its services business, a category that includes customer subscriptions to its Full Self-Driving advanced driver-assistance software. Tesla’s services business grew 33% year-over-year, bringing in $4.6 billion and accounting for a record $734 million in gross profit for the quarter.
None of this was enough to outpace Tesla’s spending on artificial intelligence projects and its Optimus robot, which took a big bite out of profits.
The company reported $787 million in net income, a 43% drop from the same period in 2025, when it earned $1.37 billion. Lower regulatory credit sales also put pressure on its profitability.
Tesla executives on the earnings call, including Musk, CFO Vaibhav Taneja, and Ashok Elluswamy, vice president of AI software at Tesla, all took bullish positions on the company’s FSD product, even as the timeline to give consumers the “unsupervised” version was delayed yet again. Today, Tesla owners can subscribe to a supervised version of the software that requires the driver to pay attention and be ready to take over at any time. The unsupervised version would be the equivalent of Level 4 autonomous driving capabilities similar to those used in robotaxis.
“We suspect somewhere around Q2 next year is when we can turn on some of the first customer vehicles to be part of the robotaxi fleet,” Elluswamy said, referring to when privately owned Tesla vehicles equipped with FSD (Supervised) would receive a software update enabling unsupervised driving.

top5.title: Nvidia's big bet on physical AI aims for safer robotaxis, humanoid robots - Ars Technica
top5.context:
Investors bullish on AI data centers may be fueling Nvidia’s multitrillion-dollar market capitalization, but the AI chipmaker has also bet billions of dollars on physical AI technologies such as robotics and self-driving cars. Part of that gambit has involved developing a full-stack safety system that companies can build upon to reduce the risk of their machines harming nearby people.
Nvidia’s Halos system launched in 2025 with hardware and software tools to help developers implement guardrails in self-driving cars and other autonomous vehicles. Then the company expanded its safety architecture to more physical AI technologies by announcing Nvidia Halos for Robotics in June 2026—with the goal of enabling safe deployments of autonomous mobile robots in warehouses, humanoid robots walking around inside a factory, or even surgical robots.
“Now the AI models are getting capable, the robot hardware is getting capable, and a thing we thought is going to be the next bottleneck is safety,” Amit Goel, head of robotics ecosystem and edge computing at Nvidia, told Ars. “So that’s why we launched our Halos for Robotics to unlock the capability of these systems.”
The expanded safety offering for robotics comes as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang described the physical AI business as already driving nearly $10 billion in annual revenue for the company during an appearance on the All-In Podcast in March 2026. Huang began highlighting physical AI as Nvidia’s second-most important growth category in 2025.
The tech giant has also invested directly in multiple robotics companies, including the humanoid robotics startups Agility Robotics and Figure AI, along with companies developing robotics foundation models. Nvidia has even partnered with the Chinese humanoid robotics company Unitree to provide an “open humanoid robot reference design” for researchers.
Expanding safety from AVs to robots
So what does Nvidia’s full-stack safety system for robotics involve? It starts with hardware, such as the Nvidia IGX Thor computing module for robotics and industrial applications that has an independent processor dedicated to safety-related workloads. “In the context of physical AI, you need to have your functional system and your safety system all running on the same silicon,” Goel said.
On the software side, the Halos operating system was designed to enable constant monitoring of “every hardware block” and “every software library” to swiftly spot any failures, Goel explained. The system also isolates safety-critical computing workloads to avoid any potential interference.
The system also includes the Nvidia Holoscan Sensor Bridge that connects sensor data with safety-related computer processing in a way that can easily identify corrupted data. This can be embedded in individual hardware components, like a microcontroller or Field Programmable Gate Array.
Last but not least, the Halos package also includes Nvidia’s simulations for testing robots in virtual environments, and an inspection lab program that allows robotics companies and other partners to get quick feedback on any safety “artifacts” that arise during robotic development.
However, adapting Nvidia Halos from autonomous vehicles to robotics required accommodating many different definitions of safety. The definition of functional safety for autonomous driving generally remains the same across different automotive companies and countries, Goel explained. But a robotic vacuum cleaning a hallway will have very different safety considerations compared to a robotic forklift handling heavy payloads in a warehouse loading dock.
“We had to reimagine and do a lot of foundational work to build a platform that is programmable, that gives all the hooks to the developers to actually define custom safety functions, but at the same time not break the underlying infrastructure that we built,” Goel told Ars. “Because giving flexibility can come at the cost of losing some control over the stack.”
Custom safety functions are also necessary because robots may operate in complex, diverse environments.
“If you are a robot coming down an aisle at six miles per hour, your senses do not see what are the blind spots and what is coming around the corner,” Gold said. “What the robots do is almost come to a halt before the turn, because they really don’t know what’s happening in all these factories, warehouses and hospitals—they’re unstructured environments and things can come from anywhere.”
Real-world robot deployments
The US startup Agility Robotics was first to incorporate Nvidia Halos into its latest Digit 5 humanoid robot, which is designed to work safely near people without requiring isolated workstations or physical barriers. The Nvidia system helped Agility bring all the relevant safety sensors and hardware inside the robot, whereas previous Digit robot operations have also relied on external sensors placed around the robot’s work cell to ensure safety.
“Now the robot is literally unchained—the safety goes with the robot wherever it goes,” Goel told Ars. “Now they can operate everywhere in a factory or a warehouse without having to set up a brand new infrastructure every time they want to do a new task.”
The Massachusetts-based robotics company Boston Dynamics has also been an early partner in the Nvidia Halos safety accreditation program, with a focus on building a safety platform that encompasses their Spot robot dogs, wheeled Stretch robots with a large robotic arm, and Atlas humanoid robots that could start deploying in the automotive factories of parent company Hyundai by 2028.
Other companies working to incorporate Nvidia Halos include the German company KION Group that deploys self-driving forklifts and other autonomous mobile robots, along with the South Korean company LG that is developing its own humanoid robot based on Nvidia’s IAI foundation model for humanoid robots called Isaac GROOT.
It remains to be seen if humanoid robots can become autonomous, general-purpose robot workers capable of handling practically any human task. But the latest push by the United States, China, and Europe to deploy more robots extends well beyond humanoids—and is putting robots to the test in many new environments.
“Earlier robots were mostly confined in one station doing one thing,” Goel said. “But in the new age of robotics with a generalized body as well as generalized skills, it is essential that the robots can do multiple tasks in multiple environments—and the only way you can do that in production is if you improve safety.”

top5.title: Self-driving Cars Could Someday Take Requests
top5.context:
This article is part of our exclusive IEEE Journal Watch series in partnership with IEEE Xplore.
The idea of letting a machine do the driving for you may put a lot of people off autonomous vehicles. But research could make it possible to backseat-drive an autonomous vehicle just as you might with a human driver.
Self-driving cars carefully balance a host of parameters to ensure a smooth ride, including things like speed, acceleration, and the smoothness of turns. But human driving preferences can often vary depending on how much of a rush they’re in, whether they’re feeling carsick, or how busy the traffic is.
These cars have a software component called the motion planner, which is responsible for choosing a safe and efficient path through traffic. The motion planner is normally tuned by engineers before the vehicles hit the road so that there’s little scope for passengers to adjust a vehicle’s driving style on the fly. But now researchers at the Delft University of Technology (TU Delft) in the Netherlands have developed a system that uses a large language model (LLM) to translate natural-language user requests such as “I am running late, go fast” into adjustments to a self-driving control system. The researchers posted their preprint on arXiv and are presenting the work at the IEEE Intelligent Transportation Systems Conference in September.
LLMs Personalize Autonomous Driving
The system doesn’t give users direct control over the vehicle’s driving decisions; it simply tunes the parameters of a safety-aware motion-planning algorithm, which helps to keep the vehicle’s behavior within safe bounds. And the system keeps the human in the loop by describing how it’s going to alter its behavior in nontechnical language, and by asking the passenger to confirm before making changes. When the system was tested in simulation, the researchers found it adjusted the speed and smoothness of driving in line with natural-language instructions.
“The motion-planning problem is not only about reaching a place while avoiding collisions, it’s also how you do it,” says lead author Diego Martinez-Baselga, a postdoctoral researcher at TU Delft. “The motivation here is trying to make the way the autonomous car drives adaptable by end users easily, just by talking to the car.”
Previous research has investigated the potential of using LLMs and video-language models (VLMs) to direct decision-making for self-driving vehicles, but the researchers deliberately targeted driving style instead. Using LLMs and VLMs to directly control vehicles faces several challenges, says Martinez-Baselga. These include relatively slow response times, which can make these models unsuitable for the fast-paced decision-making required in driving, and the fact that they can’t provide concrete performance guarantees in the way a deterministic motion planner can.
Instead, the researchers used an LLM’s language and reasoning capabilities to translate fuzzy human preferences into something a vehicle’s motion planner can use. The system relies on a model predictive-path integral controller previously developed by the researchers, which identifies multiple paths the vehicle could take to reach its goal and then judges them on various criteria, including speed, steering angle, and collision probability. It then finds an optimal path that is a combination of the trajectories that scored best on those judging criteria.
The team combined this with OpenAI’s GPT-4o-mini model to parse passengers’ natural-language suggestions and use them to tune how the controller chooses its path. The model is given the users’ prompt and a natural-language description of the scenario the vehicle is operating in. The description was handwritten by the researchers for the purposes of the study, but it could ultimately be provided directly by a car’s perception system, says Martinez-Baselga.
The model doesn’t directly tweak the settings of the controller; it uses the prompt to rate the relative importance of the judging criteria the controller uses to assess trajectories. This rating is then used to adjust each criteria up or down either side of a safe baseline set by the researchers. So, if a user says they are feeling dizzy, the LLM will dial up parameters that encourage smooth steering and gentle acceleration to make the vehicle favor more sedate travel.
Prior to making any changes, however, the model first presents the user with a natural-language description of the adjustments it plans to implement. The user can then sign off on the plan or make further suggestions. The system is also interactive, so the user can request further adjustments if the vehicle’s behavior doesn’t match expectations or the user‘s preferences change.
Martinez-Baselga says this human-in-the-loop system allows the passenger to catch instances when the model misinterprets prompts. But it also helps deal with the inherent subjectivity of suggestions like “go faster” or the possibility that models don’t accurately describe changes they plan to make. In that case the passenger can simply follow up with additional prompts “as you would do if you were in a taxi or with a friend that is driving,” says Martinez-Baselga.
The researchers tested the system in the popular self-driving simulator nuPlan in scenarios that involved merging onto a busy highway. Across eight different prompts, the system changed the controller’s parameters in ways matching user intent, with requests for a more comfortable ride dialing up smoothness and those indicating urgency leading to higher speeds.
This isn’t the first time LLMs have been used to tune a self-driving car’s motion planner. Nicolas Baumann, a Ph.D. student at ETH Zurich in Switzerland, published research last year in which an LLM tweaked the parameters of a model racing-car controller, allowing the user to alter driving style but also give more concrete instructions like “reverse the car” or “maintain a specific speed.”
The strength of the approach, says Baumann, is that separating the LLM from the main controller means that even if the model hallucinates, it can’t do anything dangerous. “You get the possibility of language interaction, but you can guarantee that it is going to be within the constraints of this classical controller, so you can bake in safety,” he says. However, setting these constraints requires considerable engineering work, he adds.
And if you want provable safety, you need to go a step further, says Matthias Althoff, a professor of cyberphysical systems at the Technical University of Munich. His group built a system that gets an LLM to suggest driving decisions, but then uses a mathematical process to check them against traffic rules and predictions about the behavior of other road users. This makes it possible to verify their safety before committing to them, something the Delft paper doesn’t provide. “As with any LLM, it is not guaranteed that the result is correct,” says Althoff. “For that reason, we safeguard the decisions of the LLM in our works.”

top5.title: Anthropic's Claude AI submitted false murder tip to Philadelphia police - Ars Technica
top5.context:
An Anthropic AI model submitted a false tip about an unsolved murder to Philadelphia police, the company and police department confirmed on Friday.
A Claude model sent the false tip on July 18 to the Philadelphia Police Department’s website for submitting information about unsolved murders, but it was flagged by a spam filter. Anthropic apparently discovered the incident on September 28 and informed the police department about it on October 8.
During internal testing, Claude Haiku 4.5 was instructed to complete various forms up to the final submission stage and to stop before submitting those forms. “Several times Claude mistakenly submitted the form instead, expecting there to be an additional confirmation page,” Anthropic said in a report describing “unintended model actions we’ve observed during evaluations and internal use of Claude.”
The false murder tip occurred when Claude Haiku 4.5 was instructed to complete tasks on randomly selected webpages, Anthropic said:
In one run, the model landed on a page referencing an unsolved homicide; that page contained a tip form run by a police department. Claude was instructed never to log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases, or submit anything destructive, but the instructions did not rule out form submissions. Claude filled out the form with the following: “I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant.”
Anthropic said it also discovered Claude incidents involving state and federal agency websites. Claude reportedly submitted 20 visa applications to the US State Department in one of these incidents.
Police call two-month delay “unacceptable”
Anthropic confirmed that the false homicide tip was sent to the Philadelphia Police Department, and the department issued a lengthy statement on the incident to the ABC station in Philadelphia. The false tip left the name and contact fields empty. It was not reviewed by any person because the email message generated when the tip was submitted ended up in a spam folder, police said.
“Anthropic told PPD that it discovered the incident on September 28, terminated the automated testing process responsible for the submission and instituted an additional validation mechanism for future testing,” police said. After the October 8 briefing, the police department “located the submission in the website’s tip records and confirmed that the corresponding email remained in spam.”
Anthropic said it informed the police department “as soon as our technical review was complete.” Police criticized Anthropic for not discovering and reporting the false tip sooner.
“The City of Philadelphia takes this incident very seriously,” the Philadelphia police statement said. “The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city’s knowledge. The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the City is unacceptable.”
Claude submitted 20 visa applications to State Department
Anthropic said the false murder tip was one of several incidents involving “websites run by US government agencies at the federal, state, and local levels. We have briefed the White House on these cases and notified each agency involved.”
A New York Times report citing anonymous sources said Anthropic’s AI agents “submitted 20 visa applications through a form available on the State Department’s website. All the applications were incomplete and were not processed.”
Philadelphia police said its normal investigative process “requires human review and vetting before any tips are disseminated for investigative follow-up… Those PPD safeguards limited the impact of this incident. They do not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting fabricated information as though it came from a person with knowledge of a homicide.”
Anthropic said it discovered the false tip and other incidents during a review of transcripts it began in July. That was the same month when Anthropic revealed that Claude had built and published a malicious Python package and carried out several attacks on other companies.
Anthropic said the review did not find any “incidents of similar severity to the cybersecurity incidents we reported this summer.” The review later moved on to transcripts of “lower-risk” testing scenarios like the one affecting the Philadelphia Police Department.
“Although the impact of these behaviors was minimal and we had already turned off live Internet access for some high-risk and cybersecurity evaluations, we have now decided to expand that to include all our internal evaluations until we have confirmed that our security and monitoring measures… reliably catch behaviors like these,” Anthropic said.
Anthropic says new tools block unintended behaviors
Anthropic said it has stopped running some evaluations and moved others to offline versions “or rebuilt them so that their tasks do not reach live websites.” The company “updated the guardrails on some of our Internet access tools, such as the web fetch tool, to heavily restrict what the model can do with them,” it said.
Anthropic said it also built new tools “to automatically detect and block the kinds of behaviors described above… When we tested it against the cases described in this post, it blocked all of them.”
The White House’s AI task force, which it calls the Super Intelligence Force, issued a statement saying it informed Anthropic “that we expect immediate and full transparency to the entities involved and the public.”
The White House AI task force also said Anthropic must “immediately provide remediation services to the affected entities and any harmed Americans,” and that all AI companies “must immediately disclose incidents involving their models and follow with swift, decisive action to remedy any and all harm,” according to an Axios report.

top5.title: Command-line tool quickly removes Apple Intelligence from macOS 27 - Ars Technica
top5.context:
A new tool is allowing Mac users the ability again to easily turn off Apple Intelligence with one click and free up to 12GB of storage.
Unlike with previous versions of macOS, macOS 27 Golden Gate doesn’t have a toggle for turning off Apple Intelligence. That makes disabling AI features that you may not want more difficult. It also means that the AI models necessary for running Apple Intelligence will take up space on your disk, even if you don’t use them or if you go through your settings to individually find and disable AI capabilities.
In response, a developer known as Om Lahore on GitHub last week created RemoveMacAI, a command-line tool that allows macOS 27 users to “turn off Apple Intelligence on macOS 27″ in a way that is “fully reversible,” per the GitHub page. They said that Apple’s Intelligence models take up “about 12GB,” but the models can actually take up over 30GB, The Verge noted.
RemoveMacAI “turns off Siri, Writing Tools, Genmoji, Image Playground, the ChatGPT extension, and all the summaries, then it deletes the models and stops macOS from downloading them again. Dictation still works because it’s a separate setting,” the developer said in a Reddit post first spotted by MacRumors.
On Reddit, RemoveMacAI’s developer said the tool is open source and further explained how it works:
It uses a configuration profile you approve in System Settings plus Apple’s own asset service, so [System Integrity Protection] stays on and nothing in /System gets touched directly. removemacai revert removes the profile, and macOS downloads the models again when you turn a feature back on.
The dev also said you can remove only the Apple Intelligence features you don’t want and keep the others.
Some users on Reddit have reported that the tool works, and it has 1,700 stars on GitHub as of this writing.
Interest in RemoveMacAI demonstrates the aversion that some users have to some or all of Apple Intelligence’s features, despite growing focus from Apple on AI-driven device and software upgrades in its computers and other devices.
“Reminds me of all the de-crufting you’ve always needed to do when you install Windows. Looks like we’ve gotten to the point on macOS too, where you need to run third-party scripts on a new OS installation to gain back control of your system resources and remove unwanted crapware,” a Hacker News user wrote in response to RemoveMacAI.
Although many users are happy to leverage Apple Intelligence in their gadgets, RemoveMacAI is a simple way for the rest to regain control over Apple Intelligence’s presence on their computers that Apple previously offered.

top5.title: How To Create iPhone Shortcuts With Apple Intelligence (And Why You Should)
top5.context:
How to create iPhone Shortcuts with Apple Intelligence (and why you should)
One of the few places where Apple Intelligence actually makes a difference.
By Adnan Ahmed
Oct. 17, 2026 9:00 am EST
Adnan Ahmed for Engadget
Shortcuts has been around since 2018 but has only recently been supercharged with AI. I'm not the biggest fan of Apple Intelligence, but its functionality in the Shortcuts app is one of the few instances where I think AI actually makes a meaningful difference to the user experience. You can already load up custom shortcuts created by other users, but Apple Intelligence now lets you create your own through natural language prompts.
If you're running iOS 27 and own an iPhone that supports Apple Intelligence, you can simply describe a shortcut and let AI do the heavy lifting for you. Launch the Shortcuts app on your iPhone. It should come preinstalled, but you can grab it from the App Store if you accidentally deleted it before. Tap on the big + icon at the bottom — this will bring up a text box where you can describe what you want the shortcut to do in plain English. Once your shortcut is assembled, tap on the play button to test it out.
How reliable is Apple Intelligence at creating shortcuts?
Adnan Ahmed for Engadget
There is a lot you can do with the Shortcuts app on the iPhone. Theoretically, everything the app allows you to automate, Apple Intelligence should be able to help you build. In practice, however, this doesn't always work and might require a bit of trial and error or manual adjustments to get the shortcut working exactly as intended. Fortunately, shortcuts created using Apple Intelligence can be edited as usual.
For instance, I described a shortcut that would switch my screen to grayscale whenever I launched Instagram and back to color when I quit the app. It did fine for the first half of the shortcut but failed to disable color filters when I exited Instagram. I went back and forth with Apple Intelligence but ended up creating two shortcuts instead.
I had fun testing the limits of the Shortcuts app and Apple Intelligence, and in my experience, the app rarely refuses to generate a shortcut altogether, even if this means putting together a solution that doesn't actually do what I asked it to.
On some occasions when I fed it an impossible prompt, the Shortcuts app acknowledged that the requested task isn't possible. Most of the time, though, it strings together actions that it thinks are good enough for the shortcut. For example, I prompted it to "turn my iPhone off when the battery goes below 20 percent," and instead it simply locked the screen. Close, but not what I was looking for.
What else can Apple Intelligence do in Shortcuts?
Adnan Ahmed for Engadget
Being able to create shortcuts using natural language is helpful, but it isn't the only improvement Apple has made to the Shortcuts app. You can also create a shortcut that leverages Apple Intelligence to generate text and make sense of data, for instance. When creating a shortcut manually, select Apple Intelligence to access the Use Model action that can send requests to an AI model, process them and generate a response. You can also use the generated response in subsequent actions within your shortcut.
You can pick between the Cloud, Cloud Pro and On-Device AI models to handle your requests. You can also choose ChatGPT to take advantage of OpenAI's models. Apple Intelligence models seem to handle text generation quite well. I described a shortcut that would fetch an article from a URL, summarize it and save it to the Notes app. You can make it so the shortcut appears as an action when you tap the Share button anywhere. To do this, launch the Shortcuts app, select your shortcut, tap on the i button and turn the Show in Share Sheet toggle on.
Once again, results can be hit or miss and depend on how well Apple Intelligence is able to understand your request and put together the necessary actions to make it work. A simple yet effective shortcut I created saved photos I took using my iPhone's telephoto camera into a separate album.
When it works, the Apple Intelligence integration within the Shortcuts app is a godsend. Just be sure to tap on Edit after generating a shortcut and double-check the actions it has put together before relying on it to do its job.

top5.title: Apple Updates App Store Rules To Ensure It Doesn't Offer AI Nudify Apps
top5.context:
Apple updates App Store rules to ensure it doesn't offer AI nudify apps
Developers are now required to filter nonconsensual intimate imagery.
By Mariella Moon
Oct. 17, 2026 8:35 am EST
Tada Images/Shutterstock
Apple has updated its moderation policy for the App Store to make sure people aren't using applications, including those that use AI tools, to "nudify" or turn normal images into sexually explicit content. The company has long prohibited pornographic materials in the App Store, and apps that were specifically made to generate sexually explicit imagery haven't been allowed for a long time. Now, Apple also wants developers to proactively police the use of their applications.
Developers with apps that host user-generated content are now required to filter nonconsensual intimate imagery, including those generated using AI tools. They must give users a way to report offensive content and block abusive accounts. They must also prevent users from being able to upload those kinds of images, and they must remove any that slip through their filters. If they fail to implement adequate safeguards of fail to remedy any violation after they had been notified, they risk being removed from the store.
In addition, it clarified its rules for apps that use bait-and-switch tactics on the company. If Apple finds that an app has misrepresented its purpose during review and that it actually has "nudification" capabilities, it will remove the app from the store and its creator from the Apple Developer Program.
